name: U’wa, variedad de Chaparral
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.

catalog_quote: Calvete (1995) propone que la variedad de Chaparral presenta una estructura silábica general (C) (C) V (C), donde es posible encontrar estructuras como V, VC, CVC, CCV y CCVC, siendo la de tipo CV la más frecuente. Sobre los rasgos prosódicos de la variedad afirma que el acento es la unidad prosódica distintiva que se realiza en el pico silábico; y en palabras de más de cuatro sílabas, plantea que puede haber hasta dos acentos, unos principal y uno secundario. Igual que Headland y Headland (1976) y Casilimas (1995), como se indicó, Calvete (1995) señala que la variedad de Chaparral cuenta con el rasgo prosódico de acentuación con una función distintiva, pero a diferencia de las demás investigaciones, no menciona la existencia de la nasalidad. ... [p. 88] Con respecto a los rasgos prosódicos con función distintiva de la lengua u’wa, todas las descripciones coinciden en que el acento es contrastivo. ... En la descripción de la variedad de Chaparral, Calvete (1995) añade que en palabras con más de cuatro sílabas puede haber más de un acento.

new_statements.translation: On the prosodic features of the variety he states that stress is the distinctive prosodic unit, realised on the syllable peak; and in words of more than four syllables he proposes that there may be up to two stresses, one primary and one secondary. Like Headland & Headland (1976) and Casilimas (1995), as noted, Calvete (1995) indicates that the Chaparral variety has the prosodic feature of accentuation with a distinctive function, but unlike the other studies he does not mention the existence of nasality.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (distinctive) in the Chaparral/Casanare (eastern, Barro Negro) variety; no placement rule is reported, so position must be treated as lexically specified until Calvete 1995 itself is read. Words longer than four syllables may carry two stresses.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Up to two stresses, one primary and one secondary, in words of more than four syllables (Calvete 1995 per Gómez Vargas 2022 p. 21).
new_statements.exceptions: None reported; the summary is a paraphrase without examples.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word; stress realised on the syllable peak. Report is a second-hand paraphrase in a literature review; the underlying thesis (Chaparral, Hato Corozal, Casanare) is not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Barro Negro Tunebo [tbn] = the eastern U'wa of Casanare (Barro Negro, Tabías, San Lope; municipios Sácama, Hato Corozal/Chaparral, Támara), called 'Chaparral-Barronegro -u'wa oriental-' by Gómez Vargas 2022 (pp. 12, 24, after Gómez 2016 and Ethnologue) and the 'Barronegro' dialect by Headland & Headland 1976. The second-hand statement (Calvete 1995) describes the Chaparral (Hato Corozal, Casanare) community, which those classifications place in tbn; Glottolog's ref 95337 leaves Calvete unassigned among the four Tunebo codes. Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description for barr1251, Rivet 1924, is a compilation whose only Casanare-area data are Fabo 1911's Manare wordlist (Manare adjoins Barro Negro on Rivet's map, p. 21); both are silent on stress. Headland 1997 (p. 16, contrastive stress, non-tonal) describes Central Tunebo [tuf] cent2150, not tbn.

tone.quote: El tono que acompaña al acento se manifiesta de dos maneras: ). La norma es tono alto (en habla normal o rápida) [”] o ascendente (en habla lenta) ('*'“] y se marca /”/. 2) Un tono descendente [ “] ocurre sobre la sílaba acentuada de algunas palabras bisílabas las … ¿cuales se acentúan en la primera sílaba, Se marca II. El núcleo de la 'sílaba donde ocurre el tono descendente es a menudo más largo que el alargamiento fonético mencionado antes, de modo que una posible interpretación alterna del tono descendente es la de un alargamiento vocálico: fáaka] [¿43dka] 'cara!,
tone.translation: The tone that accompanies the accent is manifested in two ways: 1) The norm is high tone (in normal or fast speech) [´] or rising (in slow speech) [ˇ], and it is marked /´/. 2) A falling tone [`] occurs on the accented syllable of some disyllabic words that are accented on the first syllable. It is marked /`/. The nucleus of the syllable where the falling tone occurs is often longer than the phonetic lengthening mentioned before, so a possible alternative interpretation of the falling tone is vowel lengthening: /áaka/ [àaka] 'face'.
tone.summary: Cobaría dialect: one contrastive accent per word, normally with high (or rising) tone; a falling-tone accent contrasts on some initial-stressed disyllables (áka 'piedra', àka 'cara'), maybe length.
